S062.name: Specific_Phobic_Fear
S062.description: Marked fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation that is out of proportion to the actual danger. (Note: In children, may be expressed by crying, tantrums, freezing, or clinging).

subtypes.Animal Type: Marked fear of animals or insects like dogs, bees, snakes, or spiders.
subtypes.Natural Environment Type: Marked fear of the natural environment like storms, heights, water, or the dark.
subtypes.Blood-Injection-Injury Type: Marked fear of seeing blood, receiving injections, or medical procedures.
subtypes.Situational Type: Marked fear of specific situations like airplanes, elevators, tunnels, bridges, or enclosed spaces.
subtypes.Other Type: Marked fear of other situations like choking, vomiting, loud sounds, or costumed characters.

S063.name: Immediate_Fear/Anxiety_Response
S063.description: The phobic object or situation almost always provokes immediate fear or anxiety.

subtypes.Anticipatory Anxiety: Strong anxiety triggered just by thinking about the possibility of encountering the phobic object.
subtypes.Immediate Panic Response: Overwhelming fear erupting immediately upon facing the phobic object.
subtypes.Physiological Panic Symptoms: Intense physical reactions such as heart palpitations, shortness of breath, sweating, or trembling.
subtypes.Freezing: Feeling paralyzed or unable to move due to extreme fear.

S064.name: Phobic_Avoidance_Endure
S064.description: The phobic object or situation is actively avoided or endured with intense fear or anxiety.

subtypes.Active Avoidance: Intentionally and completely staying away from contact with the phobic object or situation.
subtypes.Functional Impairment due to Avoidance: Accepting severe restrictions on daily life, job, or social activities to avoid the phobic object.
subtypes.Enduring with Distress: Forcing oneself to endure the situation while experiencing intense fear and anxiety because it cannot be avoided.
subtypes.Reliance on Safety Signals: Barely enduring the exposure by relying on a companion or safety object.

symptom.disease_info: Specific Phobia is characterized by marked, persistent fear or anxiety focused on a clearly circumscribed object or situation (e.g., animals, heights, flying, injections) that is out of proportion to the actual threat posed. Exposure to the phobic trigger almost invariably elicits an immediate anxiety response and leads to active avoidance or intense distress when avoidance is impossible, causing clinically significant interference in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. The course is often chronic if untreated, with onset typically in childhood or early adulthood, though new phobias can emerge later in life after stressful or traumatic experiences. It is distinguished from other anxiety disorders by its narrow focus on a specific stimulus rather than generalized worry, social evaluation, or unexpected panic attacks across many contexts.

patient.stressor: Eleven months ago, on an early‑morning surf session, Keith was caught in a sudden rip current that pulled him far from shore before a lifeguard reached him, an incident that shook his long‑held sense of safety in the ocean central to his Polynesian identity. At first he told himself he just needed a break, but he began turning down friends’ invitations to surf, backing out of planned trips to Maui, and even avoiding walking near the water after work, despite living minutes from the beach. The shift started to clash with his social life, his role in community cultural events that revolve around the ocean, and his own self‑image as a water‑person, fueling tension between his careful planning and impulsive efforts to distract himself with gaming or extra shifts at the shop. When he found himself unable to join a family ceremony held at the shoreline, staying in the parking lot instead, his uncle suggested he get professional help because his fear of the ocean was starting to control major parts of his life.
patient.chief_complaint: “I’ve developed this intense, irrational fear of going into the ocean, even though I grew up surfing.”
